content: 1. Diabetes mellitus (DM) in children is a metabolic disorder characterized by abnormalities in carbohydrate and lipid metabolism due to impaired insulin regulation. 2. Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), also known as juvenile-onset diabetes or insulin-dependent diabetes, is an autoimmune disease that progressively destroys insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells, eventually leading to complete insulin deficiency and dependence on exogenous insulin. 3. The exact cause and natural progression of T1DM remain incompletely understood, but genetic and environmental factors are believed to contribute to the underlying damage. 4. Genetic predisposition accounts for approximately 70-75% of susceptibility to T1DM, while environmental triggers may initiate or accelerate the autoimmune destruction of beta cells, leading to disease onset. 5. The autoimmune destruction of beta cells begins months to years before clinical symptoms such as polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) become apparent. 6. T1DM can present at any age, but most cases are diagnosed before the age of 30. 7. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is characterized by two primary defects: insulin resistance and a subsequent inability of beta cells to secrete sufficient insulin to meet increased metabolic demands. 8. T1DM results from absolute insulin deficiency, whereas T2DM involves a relative insulin deficiency. 9. Although the prevalence of T2DM in children and adolescents has increased over the past two decades, T1DM remains the most common form of diabetes in this population. 10. Chronic hyperglycemia in diabetes is associated with acute and long-term complications, including renal failure, retinopathy, neuropathy, and cardiovascular disease. 11. Advances in diabetes management, such as recombinant insulin analogs, insulin pumps, and home glucose monitoring devices, have significantly improved glycemic control in patients with diabetes. 12. However, current therapies cannot replicate the precise minute-to-minute regulation of insulin secretion seen in healthy individuals, leaving most patients with some degree of persistent hyperglycemia. 13. The historical understanding of diabetes dates back to ancient India, where it was described as honey urine due to the sweetness of the urine attracting ants. 14. In 1889, Von Mering and Minkowski discovered that removing the pancreas in dogs induced diabetes, establishing the pancreas's role in the disease. 15. The discovery of insulin in 1921 by Banting, Best, and Collip revolutionized diabetes treatment, with the first successful use of insulin in a human patient occurring in 1922. 16. The Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) in 1993 demonstrated a clear link between chronic hyperglycemia and long-term microvascular complications, emphasizing the importance of tight glycemic control. 17. T1DM is associated with genetic markers, particularly HLA haplotypes DR3-DQ2 and DR4-DQ8, which increase susceptibility, while other genes such as IL2, CD25, and PTPN22 influence disease progression. 18. 19. T2DM in children is strongly associated with obesity, insulin resistance, and certain ethnicities, including African American, Hispanic, Native American, and Asian populations. 20. Acute complications of diabetes include DKA and hypoglycemia, both of which pose significant risks of morbidity and mortality. 21. Chronic complications, such as microvascular and macrovascular damage, are related to the duration of diabetes and persistent hyperglycemia, even with treatment. 22. Glycemic control should be optimized in children with diabetes to minimize the risk of long-term complications as they age. 23. Hypoglycemia, defined as a blood glucose level below 60 mg/dL, is a frequent complication in T1DM due to the inability to match insulin delivery with minute-to-minute metabolic needs. 24. Symptoms of hypoglycemia include sweating, trembling, hunger, palpitations, headache, dizziness, and confusion, with severe cases leading to seizures or coma. 25. Mild-to-moderate hypoglycemia can be treated with 10-15 g of glucose (e.g., juice or non-diet soda), while severe cases require intramuscular or subcutaneous glucagon administration. 26. Persistent hyperglycemia (e.g., blood glucose >250 mg/dL) despite corrective insulin doses, especially with symptoms like nausea and vomiting, warrants assessment for ketonemia or ketonuria. 27. Aggressive insulin therapy is necessary to prevent progression to DKA in cases of ketosis.
